tldr: The paper proposes ToolPlanner, a two-stage reinforcement learning framework with solution path planning and dual feedback mechanisms (task completion and instruction-following), along with MGToolBench—a multi-granularity instruction dataset—to address the gap between overly detailed training instructions and real-world user behavior in tool-augmented LLMs.
contributions: Constructed MGToolBench, the first multi-granularity instruction dataset with five levels (Statement, Category, Tool, API, Hybrid) to better reflect real-world user behavior in tool-augmented LLM research.
Proposed ToolPlanner, a two-stage RL framework that uses task completion and instruction-following feedback with pairwise responses to enhance the model's tool usage abilities.
Introduced a solution path planning mechanism that provides high-level guidance during multi-round reasoning.

Demonstrated that ToolPlanner significantly outperforms SOTA models on Match Rate (+26.8%), Pass Rate (+20.2%), and Win Rate (+5.6%), with human evaluation confirming alignment of multi-granularity instructions with real-world usage habits.
methods: The authors built MGToolBench from the G3 split of ToolBench, extracting solution paths and tag lists from 4,435 seed tasks to generate 17,740 multi-level tasks (75,888 solution rounds) across five granularity levels via GPT-4 self-instruct. ToolPlanner uses LLaMA-7B as its backbone in two stages: Stage 1 trains an SFT model via cross-entropy loss to generate candidate tag lists, solution paths, and multi-round solution trees. Stage 2 applies reinforcement learning using pairwise responses scored by a reward function based on two metrics—Task Completion (Pass/Not Pass) and Instruction Following (Match/Not Match)—with rewards of 1, -1, -2, or -3. A ranking loss is combined with cross-entropy loss (L = L_l + βL_rank) to reinforce the model.
results: ToolPlanner improves Match Rate by 26.8%, Pass Rate by 20.2%, and Win Rate by 5.6% compared to the SOTA model. Human evaluation confirms that multi-granularity instructions better align with real-world user habits across plausibility, conciseness, relevance, and realness metrics. The training dataset contains 17,740 multi-level tasks and 75,888 solution rounds for Stage 1, and 98,950 paired responses for Stage 2. Tree-based decoding methods were found to perform worse on Match Rate because they sacrifice instruction-following ability.
limitations: Coarse-grained instructions (e.g., Statement or Category level) result in a larger solution space, as many APIs/tools may satisfy a single instruction.
Using only statement or category-level instructions as training data can limit model diversity and usability, as it may only interact with a few common APIs.
Tree-based decoding methods trade off instruction-following capability for higher Pass and Win Rates.
